clinicalPearls: A primary astrocyte disorder (astrocytopathy) caused by variants in GFAP, the gene for glial fibrillary acidic protein, with Rosenthal fibre accumulation in astrocytes
The adult-onset (type II) form differs from the infantile disease and presents predominantly with brainstem and bulbar dysfunction rather than macrocephaly
Characteristic features include palatal myoclonus, dysarthria and dysphagia, cerebellar ataxia, spasticity, autonomic disturbance and sleep problems

The MRI hallmark is atrophy and signal change of the medulla oblongata and upper cervical spinal cord, producing the recognisable tadpole-like appearance of a thin medulla and cord with relative preservation of the pons
Contrast enhancement or signal change of specific brainstem structures may be seen and supports the diagnosis
Most cases result from de novo dominant GFAP variants, though inherited and mosaic cases occur, so a negative family history does not exclude the diagnosis
There is no disease-modifying therapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary with attention to swallowing, airway, mobility and autonomic symptoms
reference.pathophysiology: Alexander disease is caused by dominant, usually gain-of-function variants in GFAP, which encodes the principal intermediate filament protein of astrocytes. The abnormal protein aggregates within astrocytes as Rosenthal fibres, impairing astrocyte function and disturbing their support of neurons and myelinating cells. In the adult-onset form the pathology preferentially affects the brainstem and upper spinal cord astrocytes, producing the selective medullary and cervical cord atrophy seen on imaging and the associated bulbar, cerebellar and autonomic manifestations, in contrast to the widespread frontal-predominant leukodystrophy of the infantile form.
additionalDifferentials: Multiple system atrophy with brainstem and cerebellar involvement
Multiple sclerosis and other inflammatory brainstem disease
Brainstem or foramen magnum tumour or structural lesion
Progressive bulbar palsy and motor neuron disease
Other genetic leukoencephalopathies with brainstem involvement
Chronic small-vessel or vascular brainstem disease
additionalInvestigations: Brain and cervical spine MRI to identify medullary and upper cord atrophy (the tadpole appearance) and brainstem signal change
GFAP sequencing to confirm the diagnosis, including consideration of de novo and mosaic variants
Swallow assessment (including videofluoroscopy) given the risk of aspiration
Autonomic function testing where dysautonomia is prominent
Sleep study if sleep-disordered breathing is suspected
CSF and inflammatory workup to help exclude alternative brainstem pathology
redFlags: Severe dysphagia with recurrent aspiration and pneumonia
Sleep-disordered breathing or central hypoventilation from brainstem involvement
Autonomic instability affecting cardiovascular or bladder function
Rapid bulbar deterioration compromising airway protection
reference.prognosis: Adult-onset Alexander disease is generally slowly progressive over years, with gradually worsening bulbar, cerebellar and autonomic dysfunction; the course is variable and some patients remain relatively stable for long periods. Prognosis is influenced chiefly by bulbar and respiratory involvement, which can lead to aspiration and other complications.
pitfalls: Not recognising the tadpole medullary and cervical cord atrophy as a specific pointer to the diagnosis
Excluding the diagnosis on the basis of a negative family history when many cases are de novo or mosaic
Mislabelling the presentation as multiple sclerosis or multiple system atrophy
Overlooking palatal myoclonus, a useful clinical clue to brainstem involvement
Failing to assess and protect swallowing and the airway as bulbar signs progress
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice
management: No disease-modifying treatment exists; care is supportive and directed at the bulbar, cerebellar and autonomic features
Swallow assessment with dietary texture modification and gastrostomy feeding where aspiration risk is high
Symptomatic treatment of palatal myoclonus, spasticity with antispasticity agents, and cerebellar symptoms
Management of autonomic disturbance such as orthostatic intolerance and bladder dysfunction, and sleep-disordered breathing with non-invasive ventilation where indicated
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech-and-language therapy to maintain function and communication
Surveillance for respiratory compromise and aspiration, the main determinants of prognosis, with palliative input as disease advances
Genetic counselling, noting most cases arise de novo but with a small recurrence risk from parental mosaicism
